title: LEADERSHIP | 5.24.26 The Developing SLT Checklist
author: Dominic Salles
summary: Dominic Salles argues that becoming a school leader too often means becoming a 'walking clipboard' -- managing tasks rather than solving problems of learning. He presents a five-phase decision-making framework for senior leadership teams (SLTs) that reorients every initiative toward a single question: how many extra student grades will this produce? Phase 1 (Problem Validation) demands internal data, external research (EEF Toolkit, Rosenshine, cognitive science), and comparison with schools already solving the problem. Phase 2 (Strategic Comparison and Costing) requires an ROI calculation and explicit opportunity cost analysis. Phase 3 (Scalability and Design) applies a 60-second simplicity test and plans for early failure signals. Phase 4 (Judge) uses structured voting with a 75% threshold and minority-voice protections. Phase 5 (Implementation and Iteration) adopts a 'default failure' stance -- communicating openly that the first version won't be perfect and scheduling formal reviews from week one. Throughout, Salles argues that the goal is not compliance or uniformity but genuine impact on student learning, with every task reframed as a potential solution to a learning problem.
points: * The checklist reorients every SLT decision around a single question: how many extra student grades will this produce? -- transforming tasks from compliance exercises into solutions to learning problems. * Phase 1 (Problem Validation) requires gathering internal data, consulting EEF Toolkit and cognitive science research, and identifying schools already solving the same problem before designing any intervention. * Phase 2 (Strategic Comparison and Costing) demands an explicit ROI calculation and opportunity cost analysis: what are we not doing if we fund and schedule this solution, and is the expected grade impact worth the cost? * Phase 3 applies a 60-second simplicity test to proposed solutions -- anything too complex to explain in a minute will not be implemented consistently at scale. * The 'default failure' stance of Phase 5 -- communicating openly that the first version is imperfect, scheduling week-one reviews, empowering 'problem finders' -- shifts the culture from 'the fix' to 'the evolution.'
quotes: One of the worst things about becoming a school leader is the job description. Suddenly you have a list of tasks. You can become a walking clipboard, dragging a diary around behind you like Marley's ghost.
Tasks do not build your autonomy or skills, and they don't automatically improve learning in your school. Each task can become something greater -- a solution to a problem of learning.
Leadership is making sure students learn more. Everything you do has that end goal in mind, even safeguarding.
Communicate clearly that the first version won't be perfect and will require iteration. [This] shifts the culture from 'The Fix' to 'The Evolution.'
Empower 'Problem Finders': Encourage staff to look for reasons the solution isn't working. Frame this as 'part of the process,' not a failure of leadership.
